extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of physics and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing and assessing physical theories: emphasizes grounding concepts in perceptual experience, restricting metaphysical speculation, testing models by descriptive/predictive power, and specifying domains of applicability (particles, molecules, ether-elements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid metaphysical speculation beyond perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The danger of metaphysical speculation lies in the frequency with which it contradicts our perceptual experience when it passes from the 'beyond' of sense-impression to the world of phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume conceptual constructions (e.g., higher-dimensional 'out through matter') correspond to supersensuous realities unless they symbolise perceptual experience. The 'flounder' parable illustrates that concepts intelligible within a model can be meaningless or ridiculous when projected beyond perceptual grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish conceptual constructs from phenomenal reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion is a pure conception which may describe perceptual changes, but cannot be projected into the phenomenal world without involving us in inexplicable difficulties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat entities such as particles, atoms, force, and motion as symbolic or descriptive tools rather than literal objective realities; avoid reifying geometrical or dynamical ideals as physical substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate theories by descriptive and predictive power
rubrics_metrics.description: The justification of constructs (e.g., particles, laws of gravitation) lies in the power they give us of constructing motions that describe the past and predict the future routine of our sense-impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt conceptual hypotheses only insofar as they enable accurate and economical description/prediction of perceptual experience; empirical success and predictive accuracy are the primary tests of a model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify domain of applicability for laws (scale matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: We must ask to which of the ideal corpuscles (ether-element, prime-atom, chemical atom, molecule, particle) our laws are supposed to apply; the test is whether the assumption is necessary to obtain a model enabling description of perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always state for which level/scale a law is intended; do not uncritically extend laws valid for particles to ether-elements or other levels without justification by their power to describe perceptual phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid phenomenalising mechanism (infinite regress)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phenomenalisation of the ether is useless as a means of explaining why matter moves; attempting to explain mechanism by mechanism leads to an infinite regress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not resolve explanatory problems by positing deeper untestable mechanisms ad infinitum; recognise conceptual limits and avoid replacing one unexplained 'action' with another without empirical grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require rigorous mathematical formulation for speculative extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessary mathematical equipment required for genuine research in higher-dimensioned space will act as a safeguard against over-light-hearted expeditions 'beyond the sensible'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before proposing theories that go beyond ordinary perceptual space (e.g., higher-dimensional spaces), demand substantial mathematical development and rigor to prevent unwarranted metaphysical leaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise and accept limits of scientific knowledge (say 'We don't know')
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked 'Why does matter move?' science, when pressed beyond descriptive capacities, can only reply 'We don't know.' It is better to cease supposing metaphysical explanations than to assert unfounded causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept ignorance on questions that require projecting conceptual symbols into the phenomenal world; prefer honest 'Ignoramus' answers rather than metaphysical assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate conceptual entities only if they simplify description
rubrics_metrics.description: The particle hypothesis (and similar ideals) is justified if it enables us to construct motions of groups of particles that describe and predict our sequences of sense-impressions with great and uniform accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Occam-like economy: introduce conceptual limits (particles, prime-atoms) only when they materially simplify modelling and improve descriptive/predictive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject vague or ill-defined foundational concepts (e.g., naive ether models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptions of the ether are at present very ill-defined; we are not yet satisfied with models like perfect fluid, perfect jelly, or turbulent perfect fluid for representing ether behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid building theories on poorly-defined primitives; demand clearer representation of the properties and relative motions of foundational elements before relying on them for explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise 'how' (laws of motion) over metaphysical 'why'
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of motion, in the widest sense, embrace all physical science; science may neglect the 'why' and concentrate on describing how changes of sense-impression take place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on establishing laws that capture the manner of change (how things move/behave) rather than seeking metaphysical ultimate causes that lie beyond perceptual description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anthropomorphic explanations (will, consciousness) for particle motions
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot attribute the dance of material particles to 'will' because will denotes consciousness, which cannot be logically inferred from mere material sense-impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not invoke consciousness, purpose, or will as causes for fundamental physical motions without evidence; eschew anthropomorphic causal attributions in physical theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define physical terms in terms of sense-impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Change of sense-impression is the proper term for external perception; motion is our conceptual symbolisation of this change. Matter and force are not terms expressing real problems of the phenomenal world unless tied to perceptual descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground definitions and use of physical vocabulary in perceptual phenomena; ensure terms correspond to describable sense-impressions rather than metaphysical abstractions.
